title: Sentinel Data Connectors and Event Collection

questions.sub_skill: Configure and use Microsoft data connectors for Azure resources
questions.prompt: In the Azure portal, you enable the Microsoft Defender XDR connector but clear the check box "Turn off all Microsoft incident creation rules for these products", so the rules you created earlier for Defender for Endpoint and Defender for Identity stay on. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: Defender XDR deduplicates alerts and incidents for you
The same alerts raise duplicate incidents, because the incident creation rules still turn alerts into incidents while Defender XDR also groups them into incidents
The Defender for Endpoint and Defender for Identity connectors keep ingesting the same alerts, so they are ingested and billed twice
Ingestion fails with a schema conflict between the two connectors
questions.explanation: Enabling the Defender XDR connector disconnects the individual Defender product alert connectors automatically, and Defender XDR alerts and incidents are ingested at no charge. What it does not undo, if you clear that check box, is your Microsoft incident creation rules: they still create an incident per alert while Defender XDR correlates the same alerts into its own incidents. That is why Microsoft recommends turning them off, and why the Defender portal doesn't support them at all.
why_not: Defender XDR correlates its own alerts into incidents; it does not stop separate Microsoft incident creation rules from creating more.
Microsoft disconnects the individual product connectors when the XDR connector is enabled. They may still look connected, but no data flows through them, and the alerts are free either way.
There is no schema conflict. Alert schemas do differ between the standalone and XDR connectors, which can affect existing queries, but ingestion doesn't fail.
questions.scenario_clue: "clear the check box ... incident creation rules ... stay on" - two mechanisms turning the same alerts into incidents.
questions.misconception: That leaving per-product Defender connectors on doubles ingestion and cost.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure syslog and Common Event Format (CEF) event collections
questions.prompt: A firewall vendor asks how to send logs to Sentinel. Describe the architecture and the destination table.
options: Install the Azure Monitor Agent on the appliance; events land in Syslog
Send syslog to a Linux forwarder running the Azure Monitor Agent, configured by the CEF via AMA connector; structured events land in CommonSecurityLog
Use a data collection endpoint and the Logs Ingestion API; events land in a custom table
Enable diagnostic settings on the appliance; events land in AzureDiagnostics
questions.explanation: Appliances do not run agents, so the forwarder pattern is mandatory rather than stylistic. CEF is a structured key-value extension of syslog, which is why it lands parsed in CommonSecurityLog rather than as raw text in Syslog.
why_not: Appliances do not run agents, so the Azure Monitor Agent cannot go on the appliance itself.
A firewall sending CEF uses the forwarder pattern and lands in CommonSecurityLog. The Logs Ingestion API is for sources that can call an API into a custom table.
Diagnostic settings are an Azure resource feature. A third-party appliance sends syslog instead.
questions.scenario_clue: "firewall" - an appliance that cannot run an agent; vendor security logs are usually CEF.
questions.misconception: That every log source can run the Azure Monitor Agent.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure collection of Windows Security events by using data collection rules, including Windows Event Forwarding (WEF)
questions.prompt: A requirement says to collect only specific Windows event IDs, and nothing else. Which option?
options: The Minimal predefined event set
A custom XPath query in the Windows Security Events data collection rule
A KQL transformation on the DCR
The Common predefined event set with an exclusion list
questions.explanation: All events, Common and Minimal are the predefined sets. 'Collect only these event IDs' is an XPath question. A transformation reshapes data after collection is defined; XPath decides what is collected at all.
why_not: Minimal is a predefined set chosen by Microsoft, not your list of event IDs.
A transformation reshapes data after collection is defined. XPath decides what is collected at all.
Trimming a predefined set is not how selection works. A custom XPath query names exactly the events to collect.
questions.scenario_clue: "only specific Windows event IDs, and nothing else" - a custom XPath query.
questions.misconception: That a predefined event set can be narrowed to exact event IDs.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure collection of Windows Security events by using data collection rules, including Windows Event Forwarding (WEF)
questions.prompt: Your analytics rule for suspicious logons has returned nothing for three weeks. The rule is enabled, queries SecurityEvent, and its logic is correct. What would you check on the collection side?
options: Whether an XPath filter or predefined event set removed the event IDs the rule queries
Whether those servers' events are actually being collected through Windows Forwarded Events, which writes to WindowsEvent rather than SecurityEvent
Whether the daily cap has been dropping data
Whether the workspace region matches the rule
questions.explanation: Three collection-side causes produce exactly this silence: the filter removed the event IDs; the events arrive through Windows Forwarded Events into WindowsEvent, which a SecurityEvent rule never reads; or the daily cap stopped ingestion. Region is not a property a rule depends on.
why_not: Analytics rules run in the workspace that holds the data; region does not make an otherwise correct rule return nothing.
questions.scenario_clue: "queries SecurityEvent" and "returned nothing" - check filters, which table the events land in, and whether ingestion stopped.
questions.misconception: That an empty result means nothing happened, rather than that the data never reached the table the rule reads.

questions.sub_skill: Create custom log tables in the workspace to store ingested data
questions.prompt: An application has no connector. You must retain twelve months of its verbose logs for compliance and run detections against a small subset. Describe the design.
options: One custom table in the analytics tier, with twelve months of analytics retention

A DCR-based custom table fed by the Logs Ingestion API; the detection-relevant subset in the analytics tier and the verbose telemetry in the data lake tier (for example with a split transformation), with total retention set to twelve months
Ingest everything to Syslog via a forwarder and filter at query time
Store the logs in a storage account and query them with a search job
questions.explanation: A custom source needs a DCR-based custom table and the Logs Ingestion API. Put only what detections need in the analytics tier; keep the verbose remainder cheaply in the data lake, and set total retention to cover the compliance period.
why_not: It works, but keeps twelve months of verbose data at analytics-tier prices when only a small subset feeds detections.
Syslog is for devices that speak syslog, and filtering at query time means you already paid to ingest everything.
A storage account is not a Sentinel table, so analytics rules cannot run against it.
questions.scenario_clue: "no connector", "twelve months ... compliance" and "a small subset" for detections - custom table, split across tiers.
questions.misconception: That everything retained must sit in the analytics tier.

questions.sub_skill: Create custom log tables in the workspace to store ingested data
questions.prompt: What does a KQL transformation in a data collection rule do, and what is the risk?
options: It filters at query time, so nothing is lost and cost is unchanged
It reshapes data before it is stored, so you pay for what you keep — and what it drops is gone, not hidden
It converts custom tables to the Analytics plan automatically
It applies only to Windows Security events
questions.explanation: Transformations drop columns, filter rows and normalise fields at ingestion. That is the cost lever, and it carries the same asymmetry as every other collection decision: a transformation written and never reviewed removes a field a future detection needs, invisibly.
why_not: Transformations act at ingestion, not at query time. What they drop is gone.
A transformation does not change a table's plan. It reshapes data as it arrives.
Transformations are not limited to Windows Security events. They reshape data flowing through a data collection rule.
questions.scenario_clue: "KQL transformation in a data collection rule" - it acts before storage.
questions.misconception: That a transformation only hides data at query time.
